newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turks push deeper into Iraq in pursuit of PKK.
newsitem.headline: Turks push deeper into Iraq in pursuit of PKK.

text.p: Thousands of Turkish troops, backed by tanks, heavy artillery and air power, pushed deep into northern Iraq on Wednesday in a strike against separatist Kurdish rebel bases, reports from the region said.

Witnesses said the assault, which began around 3 a.m. (2300 GMT on Tuesday) followed a security sweep by local Iraqi Kurdish authorities, who ordered all journalists to leave the border region, confiscated mobile telephones and film.
"Around 10,000 troops have crossed over from around Habur," said a Turkish official near the Habur border crossing.
He said they were heading northeast away from Zakho, the main town in the area, and had advanced up to 20 km (12 miles) into northern Iraq.
Residents on the Turkish side said about 100 tanks and armoured personnel carriers passed through the town of Cizre early on Wednesday towards to the border 45 km (30 miles) away.
"In the last month there have been coachloads of soldiers brought through the town, dozens of coaches at a time," one man told Reuters correspondent Daren Butler in Cizre.
The pro-Kurdish DEM news agency, based in Germany, said in a statement Turkish troops were bombarding hilltop positions in northern Iraq.

Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency reported clashes between troops and the Turkish separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), in a region it called Sarisarilar. It said troops backed by helicopters had inflicted heavy losses on the PKK.
The anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Concress, citing what it said were satellite telephone contacts inside Iraq, said Turkish forces had moved 80 km (45 miles) east from the town of Zakho.
The INC, based in London, said some units had penetrated all the way to the front line between the rebel-Kurdish north and Iraqi government territory. No independent confirmation was available.
Baghdad demanded a withdrawal, saying the incursion breached international law. It said there were many casualties.

"The government of the Republic of Iraq vehemently condemns this new Turkish military aggression on the sovereignty of Iraq and its territorial integrity," the Iraqi news agency INA said, quoting a Foreign Ministry spokesman.

Britain said it supported Turkey's territorial integrity but was worried by incursion. "We are urging the Turks not to exceed measures necessary to protect these interests," junior Foreign Office minister Doug Henderson said in a statement.
A Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesman said the operation was a "limited" one, in coordination with local Iraqi Kurds, to oust PKK guerrillas from the border marshes.

However, a senior security source told Reuters: "This is a wide and comprehensive operation." The border areas of northern Iraq have in the past been the scene of firefights between Turkish security forces and PKK guerrillas.
Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said the operation was a "humanitarian mission" to protect Iraqi Kurds from the PKK.
"The troops will withdraw when the operation is over," he told reporters. Turkish army officers in Iraq were tight-lipped.
A seven-km (four-mile) line of oil trucks, which regularly cross the border to buy cheap oil, extended back from Cizre. Security forces allowed no civilians beyond the town.
Military ambulances crossed Cizre on their way to Iraq. Security, always heavy in Cizre, was stepped up further.
"There is a news blackout. No member of the press is permitted access to Zakho," a local Iraqi Kurdish official said.

The Iraqi side of the border is under the general control of Massoud Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), a rival of the separatist PKK. Iraqi opposition sources said the KDP had been fighting the PKK since Monday.
Northern Iraq was set up as a Western-backed autonomous Kurdish area following the 1991 Gulf War. The KDP and another Kurdish group have shared power, if acrimoniously, since then.
Barzani teamed up last year with forces of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein against rival Iraqi Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani, prompting U.S. missile strikes against Iraqi targets.

Turkish troops regularly cross back and forth in "hot pursuit" of the PKK. In March 1995, tens of thousands of troops pushed deep into Iraq for a prolonged campaign that drove the PKK back but failed to crush them.
Security officials said troops had killed 30 Kurdish rebels in clashes in Turkey's southeast in the last two days.
More than 22,000 people have been killed in more than 12 years of fighting between the army and the PKK, which is seeking autonomy or independence in mainly Kurdish southeastern Turkey.
